11.0.0.en: 1 Also I in the first year of Darius the Mede, even I, stood to confirm and to strengthen him. 2 And now will I shew thee the truth. Behold, there shall stand up yet three kings in Persia; and the fourth shall be far richer than they all: and by his strength through his riches he shall stir up all against the realm of Grecia.

11.0.1.en: "Also I in the first year of Darius the Mede, even I, stood to confirm and to strengthen him" [1].

11.0.2.en: Some think that the talk here is of the archangel Michael supporting the archangel Gabriel, but this is not acceptable here. Rather the speaker is the archangel Gabriel, who stood beside Darius the king and strengthened him in order to support Cyrus king of Persia against Babylon. In other words, if some kings of Persia resisted God in His people, the victories they gained were by divine permission, and by a power given to them through the angels of God. Here the angel does not boast of his own power and abilities, but speaks as God's agent, and in the name of God who works through His angels.

11.0.3.en: "And now will I shew thee the truth.

11.1.0.en: Behold, there shall stand up yet three kings in Persia; and the fourth shall be far richer than they all: and by his strength through his riches he shall stir up all against the realm of Grecia" [2].

11.1.1.en: The aim of the prophecies in this chapter, which concern the two kingdoms of Persia and Greece and then the conflict between Egypt and Syria, is not to review future events that would arouse the prophet's curiosity, but to declare God's care for His Church and to urge the believers to rely on God and trust in His divine providence even in critical moments. Indeed, outwardly there appear to be worldwide conflicts between the great powers such as Babylon, Persia, Media, and Greece, and between the two halves of the Greek empire, namely the state of the Ptolemies and the state of the Seleucids; but behind these events is the hidden hand of God, who turns the whole course of affairs to the building up of His Church, and God gives His covenant with His people a special priority even if no one notices it.

11.1.2.en: Although this whole prophecy was given in the third year of Cyrus (Dan 10:1), the archangel Gabriel referred earlier to when he secretly confirmed Darius and strengthened him in his first year. This probably happened at the time when Daniel was cast into the den.

11.1.3.en: Some see that the three kings who reigned in Persia after Cyrus are: 1. Cambyses the son of Cyrus (527-522 BC): while he was on a long mission in Egypt, his younger brother Magus, surnamed Smerdis, was assassinated. 2. The so-called Smerdis (522-521 BC): he usurped the kingdom after the assassination of Smerdis, and resembled Smerdis in appearance; he married Pantaptes the daughter of Cambyses. He remained in power for 7 months and seven Magi assassinated him. 3. Darius Hystaspes or Darius I (521-486 BC) became king, and he married the same Pantaptes, the wife of the previous king, and she bore him Ahasuerus (Xerxes), who became one of the richest and most famous kings.

11.1.4.en: Others see that by the three kings the angel means Cyrus, his son Cambyses, and Darius, excluding the deceitful usurper "the so-called Smerdis".

11.1.5.en: The archangel spoke of a fourth king who surpassed the three previous kings in wealth, namely Ahasuerus the son of Darius (480-465 BC), who married Esther. St. Justin speaks of his wealth, saying that he had so many riches that even if the rivers were dried up by his forces, his wealth would not be exhausted. He crossed with an army numbering 2,641,000 persons and conquered the Greeks. The Greeks set it in their heart to avenge themselves, and they did so. He remained four years gathering his army, but the excessive size of the army deprived him of the ability to organize it, and he was defeated in the battle of Salamis. Through his pride and impetuosity Ahasuerus was defeated, and fled in a small boat, and found not one ship to rescue him, although the waters of the sea were covered with his huge fleet which he lost through his poor organization. His people counted him foolish in his military conduct, and they also despised him because he killed his brother, behaved shamefully with his sister, and committed other crimes.

11.1.6.en: The angel regarded the rest of the kings of Persia as being like those who fell. For the state of Persia declined and the spirit of the people was shattered, and the kings afterwards became as though they had no existence until Alexander the Macedonian dominated the world.

11.1.7.en: St. Jerome says: [It must be noted that after the book enumerated some of the kings of Persia after Cyrus, it clearly omitted the nine other kings and passed directly to Alexander, because the spirit of prophecy is not concerned with presenting historical details, but presents briefly only the most important events].

11.2.0.en: 3 And a mighty king shall stand up, that shall rule with great dominion, and do according to his will. 4 And when he shall stand up, his kingdom shall be broken, and shall be divided toward the four winds of heaven; and not to his posterity, nor according to his dominion which he ruled: for his kingdom shall be plucked up, even for others beside those. [3-4].

11.2.1.en: He indicates quite clearly that at the proper time Alexander the Great (356-323 BC) will arise and with great power defeat Persia and other states. We have already spoken of the enmity that Alexander the Great bore toward the Jews, but on his way to Judea he saw a vision which was fulfilled when he saw the high priest in his priestly garments receiving him with great hospitality and presenting to him the prophecies of Daniel the prophet, to assure him that he would defeat Persia and establish a great kingdom. Thereby his enmity turned into friendship, and he treated the Jews well.

11.2.2.en: He died suddenly in Babylon after successive and swift conquests and victories, but he became drunk with extreme success and wealth, and died while intoxicated. No one knows whether he died of an illness that struck him suddenly while he was drunk, for which no cure was known, or died poisoned, whether he drank the poison to commit suicide or Cassander hid it for him. The angel's saying "And when he shall stand up, his kingdom shall be broken" means that after he became the sole king of the whole East, his kingdom collapsed through his sudden death. We have already spoken of the conflicts and assassinations that took place after his death until his kingdom was finally divided among four of his commanders after the battle of Ipsus.

11.3.0.en: He says: "for his kingdom shall be plucked up, even for others beside those" [4]. This prophecy was fulfilled precisely and literally, for none of his sons inherited the throne, nor any of his relatives, but foreign commanders took the throne, although he had two sons, Heracleus and Alexander II, but neither of them took the rule; rather they were killed, one before his father's death and the other after it.

11.3.1.en: St. Jerome says: [Besides the four kingdoms, that is, Macedonia, Asia Minor, Syria, and Egypt, the kingdom of the Macedonians was torn among other, less important rulers and among petty kings of no standing. Here he refers to Perdiccas, Lysimachus, Craterus, and others who ruled Cappadocia, Armenia, Bithynia, Heraclea, Bosphorus, and many other regions that withdrew from Macedonian power and set up different kings for themselves].

11.3.2.en: All this the angel declared to Daniel the prophet many years before the birth of Alexander the Great.

11.4.s.en: 3. Prophecies about the conflict between Egypt and Syria:

11.4.0.en: 5 And the king of the south shall be strong, and one of his princes; and he shall be strong above him, and have dominion; his dominion shall be a great dominion. 6 And in the end of years they shall join themselves together; for the king's daughter of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement: but she shall not retain the power of the arm; neither shall he stand, nor his arm: but she shall be given up, and they that brought her, and he that begat her, and he that strengthened her in these times. 7 But out of a branch of her roots shall one stand up in his estate, which shall come with an army, and shall enter into the fortress of the king of the north, and shall deal against them, and shall prevail: 8 And shall also carry captives into Egypt their gods, with their molten images, and with their precious vessels of silver and of gold; and he shall refrain some years from the king of the north. 9 So the king of the south shall come into his kingdom, and shall return into his own land. 10 But his sons shall be stirred up, and shall assemble a multitude of great forces: and one shall certainly come, and overflow, and pass through: then shall he return, and be stirred up, even to his fortress. 11 And the king of the south shall be moved with choler, and shall come forth and fight with him, even with the king of the north: and he shall set forth a great multitude; but the multitude shall be given into his hand. 12 And when he hath taken away the multitude, his heart shall be lifted up; and he shall cast down many ten thousands: but he shall not be strengthened by it. 13 For the king of the north shall return, and shall set forth a multitude greater than the former, and shall certainly come after certain years with a great army and with much riches. 14 And in those times there shall many stand up against the king of the south: also the robbers of thy people shall exalt themselves to establish the vision; but they shall stumble. 15 So the king of the north shall come, and cast up a mount, and take the most fenced cities: and the arms of the south shall not withstand, neither his chosen people, neither shall there be any strength to withstand. 16 But he that cometh against him shall do according to his own will, and none shall stand before him: and he shall stand in the glorious land, which shall be wholly in his hand. 17 He shall also set his face to enter with the strength of his whole kingdom, and shall make peace with him; and he shall give him the daughter of women, corrupting her: but she shall not stand on his side, neither be for him. 18 After this shall he turn his face unto the isles, and shall take many: and a prince shall cause his reproach to cease, and moreover shall turn his reproach back upon him. 19 Then he shall turn his face toward the fort of his own land: but he shall stumble and fall, and not be found. 20 Then shall stand up in his estate one that causeth an exactor of tribute to pass through the glory of the kingdom: but within few days he shall be destroyed, neither in anger, nor in battle. 21 And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come suddenly, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries. 22 And the arms of the flood shall be swept away from before him, and shall be broken; so also the prince of the covenant. 23 And after the league made with him he shall work deceitfully: for he shall come up, and shall become strong with a small people. 24 He shall enter suddenly upon the fattest places of the land; and he shall do that which his fathers have not done, nor his fathers' fathers; he shall scatter among them the prey, and spoil, and riches: yea, and he shall forecast his devices against the strong holds, even for a time. 25 And he shall stir up his power and his courage against the king of the south with a great army; and the king of the south shall be stirred up to battle with a very great and mighty army; but he shall not stand: for they shall forecast devices against him. 26 Yea, they that feed of the portion of his meat shall destroy him, and his army shall overflow: and many shall fall down slain. 27 And both these kings' hearts shall be to do mischief, and they shall speak lies at one table; but it shall not prosper: for yet the end shall be at the time appointed. 28 Then shall he return into his land with great riches; and his heart shall be against the holy covenant; and he shall do exploits, and return to his own land. 29 At the time appointed he shall return, and come toward the south; but it shall not be as the former, or as the latter. 30 For the ships of Chittim shall come against him: therefore he shall despair, and return, and have indignation against the holy covenant: so shall he do; he shall even return, and have intelligence with them that forsake the holy covenant. 31 And arms shall stand on his part, and they shall pollute the sanctuary of strength, and shall take away the daily sacrifice, and they shall place the abomination that maketh desolate. 32 And such as do wickedly against the covenant shall he corrupt by flatteries: but the people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits. 33 And they that understand among the people shall instruct many: yet they shall fall by the sword, and by flame, by captivity, and by spoil, many days. 34 Now when they shall fall, they shall be holpen with a little help: but many shall cleave to them with flatteries. 35 And some of them of understanding shall fall, to try them, and to purge, and to make them white, even to the time of the end: because it is yet for a time appointed.

11.4.1.en: These prophecies speak of the wars of the Seleucids with the Ptolemies, for these two dynasties entered into perpetual wars against one another. By virtue of the geographical position of Palestine, in the middle between Egypt and Syria, it was in most cases the battlefield for both sides. The kings of Egypt were called the kings of the south, and the kings of Syria the kings of the north.

11.4.2.en: It is fitting for us to realize that this section covers a long period of time, about two centuries, and when it speaks of the king of the north or the king of the south it does not mean one particular king for each of the two states.

11.5.0.en: "And the king of the south shall be strong,

11.5.1.en: and one of his princes; and he shall be strong above him, and have dominion; his dominion shall be a great dominion" [5].

11.5.2.en: The first king of the south (Egypt) was strong, he and his wife; he was Ptolemy Lagus (the First, 323-285 BC). He was strong, intelligent, and rich, stronger than Antiochus the son of Seleucus, king of the north (Syria), but afterwards Antiochus became stronger and richer, since he annexed Babylonia and Media. The angel knew the greatness that Antiochus would attain, more than Ptolemy, in the future.

11.5.3.en: As for who is meant by one of his princes who became stronger than he and had greater dominion, St. Jerome says of him:

11.5.4.en: [The person mentioned here is Ptolemy Philadelphus, the second king of Egypt, and the son of the Ptolemy previously mentioned. It is said that in his reign the seventy translated the Holy Bible into Greek.

11.5.5.en: He also sent many treasures to Jerusalem to Eleazar the high priest, and sent vessels for the Temple.

11.5.6.en: The keeper of his library was Demetrius of Phalrum, a man of fame among the Greeks as an orator and philosopher.

11.5.7.en: It is reported of Philadelphus that he was of great power which surpassed that of his father Ptolemy, for history relates of him that he had 200,000 foot soldiers, twenty thousand horsemen, two thousand chariots, and four hundred elephants, the first to import them from Ethiopia...

11.5.8.en: His treasure of gold and silver was very great, and his annual income which he received from Egypt amounted to 14,800 pieces of silver, and the wheat from half a million to a million ardebs].

11.6.0.en: "And in the end of years they shall join themselves together; for the king's daughter of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement: but she shall not retain the power of the arm; neither shall he stand, nor his arm: but she shall be given up, and they that brought her, and he that begat her, and he that strengthened her in these times" [6].

11.6.1.en: He prophesies of the latter days, when a treaty was made between the kings of Egypt and Syria in 250 BC, and the means of this treaty was the marriage of the king of Syria to the daughter of the king of Egypt. Indeed, Antiochus Theos (285-247 BC), the third king of Syria, divorced his wife Laodice to marry Berenice, or Betonice, or Bernice, the daughter of Ptolemy II (283-246 BC), the one called Philadelphus. He gave his daughter thousands of pieces of gold and silver without number as a dowry for her, so that he was called Phernophoros, that is, "the dowry-giver" Dowery-giver (dotalis). Ptolemy's aim was to use the marriage of his daughter to the king of Syria as an opportunity to gain control over Syria and the whole kingdom of Antiochus, but the plan failed. For Laodice, whom Antiochus kept after divorcing her as one of his concubines and not as queen, stirred up her friends against the king, and killed her rival Berenice and those around her. Antiochus took back his first wife Laodice, who, it is said, killed him by poison shortly afterward, and she set her elder son Seleucus Callinicus on the throne, and the younger son, Antiochus the Younger, called Hierax, as governor over Asia Minor. It is said that the elder son was the one who won over Berenice and promised her that he would care for her, so she was reassured by him, and he killed her and her son in a vile and hideous way. Thus, since deceit entered the lives of the two kings, both failed.

11.6.2.en: The prophecy was fulfilled literally, for the plan of the king of Egypt failed completely: on the one hand the king did not attain his goal by giving his daughter as wife to the king of Syria, and the daughter was killed along with those around her, and also her husband who had been her support, and her son was killed as well.

11.7.0.en: "But out of a branch of her roots shall one stand up in his estate, which shall come with an army, and shall enter into the fortress of the king of the north, and shall deal against them, and shall prevail:

11.7.1.en: And shall also carry captives into Egypt their gods, with their molten images, and with their precious vessels of silver and of gold;

11.7.2.en: and he shall refrain some years from the king of the north.

11.7.3.en: So the king of the south shall come into his kingdom, and shall return into his own land" [7-9].

11.8.0.en: He indicates that a branch of the family of Bernice will come and defeat the king of the north. Indeed, Ptolemy (III) Euergetes, the brother of Berenice, probably younger than she, the third king of Egypt who succeeded his father Philadelphus, gathered a great army to avenge his sister. And indeed he defeated Callinicus, who was ruling Syria jointly with his mother Laodice, and conquered many fortified cities. He not only triumphed over Syria, but also stormed Cilicia and some regions beyond the Euphrates, and almost gained dominion over all of Asia. News came of a rebellion arising in Egypt, which made Euergetes hasten back to Egypt carrying with him the captives and also two and a half thousand statues of gold and silver, some of which Cambyses had brought from Egypt long before, and he also carried 40,000 talents of silver. Callinicus did not think of entering into another battle with Euergetes, for he knew that he could not defeat him or recover what he had carried off as spoil. Euergetes remained king for 46 years [8]. When Callinicus felt defeated before Euergetes he appealed for help to his brother Hierax, governor of Asia Minor, who paid no heed to his brother's cries, for he reckoned that he was more entitled to the throne. Later he entered into a battle with his brother, and his brother fell dead from his horse, while Euergetes remained king in Egypt for 4 years after the death of the king of Syria. In any case Euergetes did not return to Syria.

11.9.0.en: "But his sons shall be stirred up, and shall assemble a multitude of great forces: and one shall certainly come, and overflow, and pass through: then shall he return, and be stirred up, even to his fortress.

11.9.1.en: And the king of the south shall be moved with choler, and shall come forth and fight with him, even with the king of the north: and he shall set forth a great multitude; but the multitude shall be given into his hand" [10-11].

11.10.0.en: He prophesies of the two sons of Callinicus king of Syria, Seleucus (II) Ceraunus and Antiochus the Great, who gathered an army to take revenge on the Egyptians after the death of Euergetes. But Ceraunus was killed in Phrygia in the third year of his reign, betrayed by Nicanor and Apaturius while he was preparing for the battle against Egypt, leaving the rule to his brother alone. Antiochus the Great became a distinguished king and led a huge army against Egypt. At that time Ptolemy Philopator was the fourth king of Egypt, and he bore the title Philopator as a mark of disgrace, because the word means "lover of his father", while he killed his father, his mother, and his brother, so the people hated him. This is what drove Antiochus the Great to enter with him into a fierce battle at Raphia in 217 BC, in which both sides used huge elephants, to recover what Syria had lost, regarding the people's hatred of their king as an opportunity for victory. But the king of Egypt gathered a great army almost equal to the army of Syria. Ceraunus was able to move with his army and recover the seized Syrian lands, while the king of Egypt, characterized by cowardice and negligence, was preparing with his great army, and when he met the army of Antiochus he defeated it in a great slaughter [11].

11.10.1.en: Philopator did not defeat Antiochus the Great by his courage and strength, but the Lord permitted this to break the pride of the latter.

11.11.0.en: And since he was negligent in following up his victory, especially as he did not trust those around him, in spite of his victory he made peace with Antiochus in an ungenerous manner [12].

11.11.1.en: "And when he hath taken away the multitude, his heart shall be lifted up; and he shall cast down many ten thousands: but he shall not be strengthened by it" [12].

11.11.2.en: The historians say that Philopator could easily have seized Syria, but he was given over to his bodily lusts and the dissolution of his character, along with his committing many crimes. For on his return from the war he killed his wife Eurydice and committed many crimes, and he also handed the reins of the kingdom to a wicked woman, a musician called Agathoclea, and he fell in love with her brother Agathocles, whom he set up as commander-in-chief over Egypt.

11.11.3.en: After he became famous for victories, so that the whole East feared him, he plunged into drunkenness with idleness and slackness, and nothing occupied him any longer except banquets, revels, and pleasures; thereby his heart was lifted up to the clouds of his victories, only to fall cast down in shame.

11.11.4.en: "For the king of the north shall return, and shall set forth a multitude greater than the former, and shall certainly come after certain years with a great army and with much riches.

11.12.0.en: And in those times there shall many stand up against the king of the south: also the robbers of thy people shall exalt themselves to establish the vision; and they exult" [13-14].

11.12.1.en: Here the angel declares to the prophet the rise of new wars, for after the death of Ptolemy Philopator, Egypt was without a king, since his son Ptolemy Epiphanes (the Fifth, 203-181 BC) was a small child four years old, and the perversion and arrogance of Agathocles increased greatly, so the provinces subject to Egypt rose up and rebelled against the rule, and entered into great internal troubles. Antiochus attacked Egypt, and since Egypt had become very weak it sent an embassy to Rome, and since the Romans desired to extend their dominion in the world, they sent to Antiochus asking him to stop the war. After many attempts he failed in his war, and finally he triumphed in a battle against the Egyptian commander Scopas on the border of Judea. The angel made clear that Antiochus the Great did not stand alone against Egypt, but Egypt came to have many enemies.

11.12.2.en: Antiochus made a treaty with Philip III of Macedon, and asked the help of the Jews [13]. The pious among the Jews refused to help him, but some Jews supported him.

11.12.3.en: What do we mean by the robbers of the people of Daniel who exalt themselves to establish the vision? St. Jerome sees in this a prophecy about the high priest Onias the Younger, who betrayed the altar of the Lord and defiled it in Jerusalem. He fled to Egypt taking with him a great number of Jews, and Ptolemy received him with great honor. The king gave him the region of Heliopolis (New Egypt), and there he built an altar to the Lord, claiming that he was fulfilling the prophecy of Isaiah the prophet concerning the setting up of an altar to the Lord in the land of Egypt (Isa 19:19), as the Book of Maccabees tells us and also the historian Josephus. St. Jerome says: [The temple remained standing until the time of Vespasian for 250 years. The city itself was called "the city of Onias", and it was destroyed during the war between the Jews and the Romans. No trace of the temple or of the city remained in the days of St. Jerome.

11.12.4.en: "So the king of the north shall come, and cast up a mount, and take the most fenced cities: and the arms of the south shall not withstand, neither his chosen people, neither shall there be any strength to withstand.

11.12.5.en: But he that cometh against him shall do according to his own will, and none shall stand before him: and he shall stand in the glorious land, which shall be wholly in his hand.

11.13.0.en: He shall also set his face to enter with the strength of his whole kingdom, and shall make peace with him; and he shall give him the daughter of women, corrupting her: but she shall not stand on his side, neither be for him" [15-17].

11.14.0.en: St. Jerome says that Antiochus, in order to recover Judea and some cities of Syria, entered into a battle with Scopas, the commander of Ptolemy, beside the Jordan near a city called Peneas, and Scopas fled, but he was besieged in Sidon with ten thousand of his soldiers. The Egyptians no longer had strength to resist, and so he sat in the glorious land, Palestine, which came under his dominion; in the Septuagint it reads "the land of desire", by which is meant the land in which God delights. God had declared beforehand to Daniel what would happen, so that when Palestine fell into the hands of the violent Antiochus, the spirit of the pious would not be shattered, but they would realize that God had declared this beforehand. Thus this prophecy becomes a cause of comfort to them in the midst of distress and of falling under suffering and persecution. And in order to bring Egypt into his grasp, Antiochus gave his beautiful daughter Cleopatra to the young Ptolemy, thinking that by this he would subject Egypt to his dominion. But she did not stand by him [17], but stood by her husband, so he turned his face from Egypt to Asia Minor with his naval fleet and captured many of the isles.

11.15.0.en: "After this shall he turn his face unto the isles, and shall take many: and a prince shall cause his reproach to cease, and moreover shall turn his reproach back upon him" [18].

11.15.1.en: By the isles are meant Asia Minor, the coasts of the Mediterranean, Greece, Cyprus, and all the islands in the sea. For it was the custom of the Jews to call all the regions lying beyond the sea "isles", since they had no experience of maritime affairs.

11.15.2.en: Antiochus was able, with a small army, to advance into Asia Minor, and with him was Hannibal, whose fame had reached the Romans and who were terrified of him, so it was not difficult for him to drive the Romans out of every region he crossed into. Hannibal became an intimate friend of Antiochus, accompanying him every day and speaking with him, but Antiochus doubted his loyalty. Antiochus headed toward Greece without good planning and without caution, and when he reached Chalcis he was attracted to a beautiful girl there and held a wedding feast with her as though he were in his own land in perfect peace. By virtue of his great fame he opened many cities that were terrified before him, and freed these cities from the Romans. And as the angel declares to Daniel: "After this shall he turn his face unto the isles, and shall take many" [18].

11.15.3.en: By rejecting the counsel of Hannibal, Antiochus began to collapse and disgrace came upon him without his knowing, and he mocked the Romans and reproached them. He first occupied some regions in Greece that were allied with the newly emerging Roman power, but the Roman commander Acilius, or Lucius Scipio Nasica (with his brother Publius Scipio Aficanus), was able to draw him beyond Mount Taurus and defeat him at Magnesia, and so he turned back on Antiochus the reproaches that he used to utter against the Romans; therefore the angel declares "and a prince shall cause his reproach to cease, and moreover shall turn his reproach back upon him" [18]. Thereby Antiochus collapsed before Greece allied with Rome. And here many blame the commander Scipio because he left all the resources of Rome at the disposal of Philip of Macedon.

11.16.0.en: "Then he shall turn his face toward the fort of his own land: but he shall stumble and fall, and not be found" [19].

11.16.1.en: Antiochus weakened before the Roman commander Scipio, and returned to his country in disappointment to fortify himself in his land after losing many [19], and when he tried to plunder the temple of Jupiter Dodoneus in Elymais near Susa, perhaps to pay the Roman tribute, he and his soldiers were killed by the people who rose in revolt against him. Therefore the angel says "he shall fall, and not be found".

11.16.2.en: Antiochus died in 187 BC. After him reigned Seleucus Philopator (187-176 BC), whom some call Ceraunus, and the second son was Demetrius. The third was Antiochus Epiphanes. Now he speaks of his successor Seleucus, saying:

11.17.0.en: "Then shall stand up in his estate one that causeth an exactor of tribute to pass through the glory of the kingdom: but within few days he shall be destroyed, neither in anger, nor in battle?" [20].

11.17.1.en: His son Seleucus Philopator succeeded him, and he was excessive in demanding taxes [20] to pay the tribute to Rome, so he sent his prime minister Heliodorus to Jerusalem to plunder the Temple there. Soon afterward Heliodorus assassinated his master, and Antiochus Epiphanes took the rule.

11.18.0.en: "And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come suddenly, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries" [21].

11.18.1.en: All the historians agree that Antiochus Epiphanes was cunning and violent to the utmost degree. When news of his father's death reached Rome, they released him, since they were content (they made light of) with his brother Demetrius. He flattered the Romans, and when he reached his country they received him with great hospitality. His brother Seleucus did not last long, and had left his son as his successor, but Antiochus by his deceit was able to take the rule without right; therefore the angel says of him: "to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom" and continues "and obtain the kingdom by flatteries". How was that done? By his deceit he pretended to be a man of peace with his nephew, the lawful heir to the kingdom, and that he was his guardian... Thereby he was able to take the kingdom from him.

11.19.0.en: "And the arms of the flood shall be swept away from before him, and shall be broken; so also the prince of the covenant" [22].

11.19.1.en: Antiochus found resistance from his own people, who discovered his deceit and his exclusion of his nephew, and he also found trouble from the surrounding countries such as Egypt, for its king Ptolemy Philometor was a boy, and his advisers were on good terms with the son of Seleucus whom his uncle had excluded, so they sent secret help to resist Antiochus. Many neighboring countries did likewise. But all these resisting arms were broken, as the angel says here, for they were like a sweeping flood. Yet they went before him and collapsed. This was not because of the strength of Antiochus but by divine permission, for God permitted his rising to discipline the Jews at that time.

11.19.2.en: Who is the prince of the covenant who was broken before Antiochus? Ptolemy is meant, because he is related by kinship to the lawful heir, the son of Seleucus.

11.19.3.en: This Ptolemy Philometor was the son of Ptolemy Philopator and Cleopatra the sister of Seleucus, and although he was a small boy who could not move by himself, he was a prince of the covenant by being king of Egypt.

11.20.0.en: "And after the league made with him he shall work deceitfully: for he shall come up, and shall become strong with a small people" [23].

11.20.1.en: At first Antiochus was despised in Syria, and there were attempts, supported by Egypt, for the lawful king "the son of Seleucus" to take the rule. But Antiochus sent to the king of Egypt (his sister's son) asking for his friendship, especially as Cleopatra, the sister of Antiochus, was still alive. Ptolemy was reassured by his uncle Antiochus and they became friends, but when Antiochus had established his footing he suddenly launched a campaign of a small number and seized some cities of Egypt from his nephew, who did not expect this campaign.

11.20.2.en: "He shall enter suddenly upon the fattest places of the land; and he shall do that which his fathers have not done, nor his fathers' fathers;

11.21.0.en: he shall scatter among them the prey, and spoil, and riches: yea, and he shall forecast his devices against the strong holds, even for a time" [24].

11.21.1.en: By his deceit, and not by a huge military force, he was able to seize some of his cities from his nephew and plunder them and carry spoil and wealth to his country, since the Egyptians lived in luxury. Antiochus went back thinking how he would afterward attack the fortified land of Egypt as a second stage.

11.21.2.en: Antiochus surpassed his fathers and forefathers in deceit, and there was none to compare with him, especially as the breaking of covenants - especially in the East - is considered shameful, whatever the circumstances.

11.22.0.en: "And he shall stir up his power and his courage against the king of the south with a great army; and the king of the south shall be stirred up to battle with a very great and mighty army; but he shall not stand: for they shall forecast devices against him" [25].

11.22.1.en: After seizing the open, secure cities and plundering them, Antiochus went back to prepare a huge army to conquer Egypt and attack its fortified cities. He needed a long time to form this army after having seized many neighboring countries by his deceit. At the same time his nephew perceived his uncle's inclinations, so he prepared for open battle and equipped himself with a great army. [21-25] focused on Antiochus Epiphanes, who was referred to before in chapter 8, and who was called "the Antichrist of the Old Testament period".

11.22.2.en: The men of his palace called him Epiphanes, that is, the exalted or the glorious, because he was concerned with the arts and architecture and with building huge, beautiful, and glorious edifices, but some changed one letter, Epimanes, which means "the madman", because he was violent, deceitful, and deranged in his conduct.

11.23.0.en: "Yea, they that feed of the portion of his meat shall destroy him, and his army shall overflow: and many shall fall down slain" [26].

11.23.1.en: God permitted Ptolemy to be defeated before Antiochus through the betrayal of his men, because he was absorbed in pleasures, covetous, and heedless of the affairs of his country.

11.24.0.en: "And both these kings' hearts shall be to do mischief, and they shall speak lies at one table; but it shall not prosper: for yet the end shall be at the time appointed" [27].

11.24.1.en: The two kings, the uncle and his nephew, were wicked and deceitful, so when Ptolemy was broken the two saw their need of reconciliation and of entering into friendship, so that each might plan for the other what would destroy him. Antiochus had defeated his nephew but did not dare to complete the journey, for he feared collapse before the rest of the fortified cities. The two sat at one table, but their hearts were full of hatred and enmity. Thus politics does to many, so that a person loses his trust in those nearest to him.

11.24.2.en: The angel says: "for yet the end shall be at the time appointed" [27], meaning that what happened was within certain limits, so that God's plan might be fulfilled, for the end had not yet come, but God has appointed a time for everything.

11.25.0.en: "Then shall he return into his land with great riches; and his heart shall be against the holy covenant; and he shall do exploits, and return to his own land" [28].

11.25.1.en: Antiochus returned to his land, Syria, and did not possess Egypt, but he carried much wealth from it, then returned to wage war against Jerusalem and the holy Temple, and against all the Jews. He was compelled to leave Jerusalem, as he left many treasuries, as it is written in (2 Macc 5:2), where God wrought wonders. He added what he had seized from the Temple to what he had plundered from Egypt, and returned to Syria carrying within him the desire to resist the holy covenant, that is, to resist God Himself.

11.25.2.en: "At the time appointed he shall return, and come toward the south; but it shall not be as the former, or as the latter.

11.26.0.en: For the ships of Chittim shall come against him: therefore he shall despair, and return, and have indignation against the holy covenant: so shall he do; he shall even return, and have intelligence with them that forsake the holy covenant" [29-30].

11.26.1.en: When the treaty was made between Antiochus and his nephew and they sat together at one table, without cause Antiochus prepared his army and broke the covenant and entered Egypt and seized part of it, and he besieged Alexandria and took the boy king captive. At that time a Roman mission came headed by Publuis or Popilus from Chittim, by which is meant Macedonia, Greece, and Italy. Antiochus received him very kindly as was his custom, but Publius was not deceived; rather he demanded of him, by order of the council of the Senators or Roman elders, that he leave Egypt at once. He asked him for a delay to consult with his friends and advisers, but Publius firmly drew a circle around the king with the staff in his hand, and asked him to call his advisers and come to an understanding with them at once before going out of the circle, or else he would declare war against him immediately. Antiochus could not hesitate, but surrendered himself into the hands of the Senator and turned back from Egypt. This historical fact the angel declared to Daniel the prophet.

11.26.2.en: Antiochus did not achieve his ambitions in Egypt, and returned in shame merely at a word from the Roman Senator, so he turned back to direct all his energies against Jerusalem and the holy Temple; this time he came to Jerusalem more violently and fiercely than the previous time. He went back seeking traitors to the Temple, among the Jews, who "forsake the holy covenant", to use them against the Jewish people and the divine holy things. This was fulfilled as is described in detail in (2 Macc 3-5).

11.27.0.en: "And arms shall stand on his part, and they shall pollute the sanctuary of strength, and shall take away the daily sacrifice, and they shall place the abomination that maketh desolate" [31].

11.27.1.en: The arms that stood in support of Antiochus are those who betrayed God and forgot the Law, so they were supporters of the wicked king against divine truth (2 Macc 4).

11.27.2.en: The Jews wrongly heard that Antiochus had been killed and rejoiced greatly, and when he heard of the matter on his way back he passed through Jerusalem and dealt with them very harshly.

11.27.3.en: The Jews took refuge in Rome for support, so Rome sent an army while Antiochus turned to resist the Jewish forces under the leadership of the Maccabees [29]. Antiochus submitted to Rome and promised to keep the peace, but as soon as the Roman forces returned he betrayed the promise [30], and some traitors from the Jews helped him in that.

11.27.4.en: With his known deceit he did not prevent the worship of the living God, but he began first by practicing pagan worship inside the Temple side by side with the worship of God. He defiled the Temple by placing in it the statue of Jupiter Olympius, then afterward he stopped the Jewish worship, set himself up as a god, and sacrificed a pig on the altar. The faithful pious rose up against him under the leadership of the heroic family of the Maccabees, and thousands of them were killed. What he did is reckoned "the abomination of desolation of the Temple", a type of the abomination of desolation that will occur at the end of the ages, to which the Lord Christ referred (Mt 25:24).

11.27.5.en: "And such as do wickedly against the covenant shall he corrupt by flatteries:

11.28.0.en: but the people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits" [32].

11.28.1.en: The angel makes clear how the priests and also the people were divided into two groups, one group deceived by the flatteries of Antiochus, and another who held fast to the knowledge of God, so God grants them more strength and understanding. As St. Jerome says: [No one doubts that this will also happen in the days of the Antichrist, when many will resist him and flee from him in many directions. The Jews interpret these things as concerning the destruction of the Temple at the hands of Vespasian and Titus, and they say that many of those whom he raised up knew their Lord and were killed for keeping His Law].

11.28.2.en: St. Jerome says: [We read in the Maccabees that there were those who pretended to be guardians of the Law of God, and finally entered into a covenant with the Gentiles... But in my opinion this will happen in the days of the Antichrist when the love of many will grow cold. Of these our Lord says in the Gospel, "Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?" (Lk 18:8)].

11.28.3.en: "And they that understand among the people shall instruct many:

11.28.4.en: and they glory in the sword, and in flame, in captivity, and in spoil, many days.

11.29.0.en: Now when they shall fall, they shall be holpen with a little help: but many shall cleave to them with flatteries" [33-34].

11.29.1.en: The wise among the people (probably of the priests) rejected the flatteries of Antiochus and taught many to despise all means of torment, whether killing by the sword or burning with fire or their captivity or the plundering of their possessions, reckoning all these as glories and honor.

11.29.2.en: Here is a call to follow the loyal and the faithful in their relationship with God, and not to be led after flatterers whatever their rank or position. It is also a call to the priests and leaders to accept the sword and despise the fire, and not to lose their loyalty to God and their adherence to the divine commandment, for even if they seem to have fallen, and there is no help but a little, like the Maccabees to whom only a very few faithful clung, they must not care about temporal glories and praise.

11.29.3.en: "And some of them of understanding shall fall, to try them, and to purge, and to make them white, even to the time of the end:

11.30.0.en: because it is yet for a time appointed" [35].

11.30.1.en: Here he affirms that some of the understanding will fall, and perhaps he means here falling by the sword or by burning with fire, but this does not mean that God does not support them; rather He permits this for their salvation, for their approval in the end, where they are purged and made white by the work of God in them during their suffering in tribulation. They are counted martyrs who passed through the fires and were refined like pure gold.

11.30.2.en: Thus God was preparing the souls of the Maccabees and those like them not from the moment of their birth, but even before their creation... so that when they moved to action and saw the resistance, they would return to the prophecies of Daniel and be strengthened and not fear.

11.30.3.en: St. Hippolytus of Rome says: [Antiochus became king over Syria, reigning in the year 107 of the kingdom of Greece. At the same time he stirred up war against Ptolemy king of Egypt, defeated him, and gained dominion. On his return from Egypt he went up to Jerusalem in the year 103, carrying with him all the treasures of the house of the Lord, and headed to Antioch. After two years the king sent a collector of taxes to the cities of Judea to compel the Jews to abandon the laws of their fathers and subject them to the statutes of the king. He came and tried to compel them to this, saying: "Come forth, and do the commandments of the king, and you shall live." But they answered: "We will not come forth, nor will we do the king's commandments; we shall die pure"; so he slew a thousand souls (1 Macc 2:33). Thereby was fulfilled what Daniel said: "and they shall stumble by toils and famine and sword and captivity" (Dan 11:33). And Daniel adds: "they shall be holpen with a little help" (Dan 11:34). For Mattathias arose at that time, and Judas Maccabeus, to help them and deliver them from the hands of the Greeks].

11.30.4.en: Suddenly the vision turned to the end of times and the coming of the Antichrist, in a detailed account of his person and his wicked works.

11.31.s.en: 4. The end of times - the Antichrist:

11.31.0.en: 36 And the king shall do according to his will; and he shall exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak marvellous things against the God of gods, and shall prosper till the indignation be accomplished: for that that is determined shall be done. 37 Neither shall he regard the God of his fathers, nor the desire of women, nor regard any god: for he shall magnify himself above all. 38 But in his estate shall he honour the God of forces: and a god whom his fathers knew not shall he honour with gold, and silver, and with precious stones, and pleasant things. 39 Thus shall he do in the most strong holds with a strange god: whoso knoweth him he shall increase with glory, and he shall cause them to rule over many, and shall divide the land for a reward. 40 And at the time of the end shall the king of the south push at him: and the king of the north shall rise up against him with chariots, and with horsemen, and with many ships; and he shall enter into the countries, and shall overflow and pass through. 41 He shall enter also into the glorious land, and many shall stumble: but these shall escape out of his hand, even Edom, and Moab, and the chief of the children of Ammon. 42 He shall stretch forth his hand also upon the countries: and the land of Egypt shall not escape. 43 But he shall have power over the treasures of gold and of silver, and over all the precious things of Egypt: and the Libyans and the Ethiopians shall be at his steps. 44 But tidings out of the east and out of the north shall trouble him: therefore he shall go forth with great fury to destroy, and utterly to make away many. 45 And he shall plant the tabernacles of his palace between the seas and the glorious holy mountain; yet he shall come to his end, and none shall help him. [36-39] presents the same person mentioned in (Dan 7:8; 9:26) as the "little horn"; here he calls him the king who does according to his will [36].

11.31.1.en: "And the king shall do according to his will; and he shall exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god, and shall speak marvellous things against the God of gods, and shall prosper till the indignation be accomplished: for that that is determined shall be done.

11.31.2.en: Neither shall he regard the God of his fathers, nor the desire of women, nor regard any god: for he shall magnify himself above all" [36-37].

11.31.3.en: The Jews differed in their interpretation of the preceding text; some thought that the angel is speaking of Antiochus Epiphanes, and others thought that the talk here is about the Romans such as Vespasian and his son Titus, or the Roman state as a whole. But the Fathers of the Church saw that the talk here is about the Antichrist and not about Antiochus, because what follows does not apply to him. Yet some saw that the talk is about the arrogant Roman state, in which some emperors set themselves up as gods and demanded that the people bow down to their statues and images.
